title: Franklin missed the Nobel not just because she died young
dek: She shot Photo 51 and was the first to see that DNA's two forms interconvert; but what really got her undercredited by history was King's College's refusal to share information, while Cambridge shared.
why: This is a rebroadcast from the BBC archive, medium information density, but the three guests explain Photo 51, A-form and B-form DNA, and the Nobel rules more clearly than most popular science.
who: Readers interested in the history of science, the situation of women in research, and how DNA was discovered; anyone wanting to understand how Nobel rules and lab politics shape credit allocation.
skip: The first two minutes or so are ads and show introductions for other BBC podcasts; skippable.

points.h: Cambridge gave women a diploma, not a degree
points.body: Franklin entered Cambridge in 1938 to read natural sciences; at the time women across the university were capped at 500, confined to the two women's colleges, Newnham and Girton. She sat every exam and took a first in one year, but the university did not award degrees to women, only a diploma, and she never attended a graduation ceremony. Patricia Farrar points out that what was truly hard was not the number of men but the attitude of "you don't belong here" — at Cambridge they were merely "a presence," not ordinary students.

points.h: She turned coal from mysticism into something testable
points.body: In wartime, coal decided Britain's electricity and railways, but no one could say clearly why coal from different mines behaved differently. Franklin used gas to probe coal's porosity and found that some pores could only admit small molecules like helium while others admitted larger ones; when heated, some coal turned to graphite and some to a glass-like "glassy carbon," the latter extremely valuable. Jim Naismith says her work let the mines predict how a given coal would behave under specific conditions from a sample, without having to dig it out and try it first. These were single-author papers during and after her PhD, and were recognized as her achievement at the time.

points.h: One DNA photo took 100 hours of exposure
points.body: Judith Howard describes the equipment of the day: X-ray tubes were fairly primitive, Franklin had to clean diffusion pumps herself with buckets of benzene to maintain vacuum, cameras were often homemade, and the sample — a lump of coal, a crystal or a fibre — had to be held by hand and aligned with the beam. Data could only be recorded on photographic film, and some of her later exposures of DNA fibres ran about 100 hours. Today data is collected digitally, computers are fast, and instruments are made by companies, but Howard stresses this is not a different science, only a different way of doing it.

points.h: One letter planted the hostility between her and Wilkins
points.body: Franklin was hired to study proteins, then informed by a letter that she would switch to DNA, and then informed she would work with a PhD student, Ray Gosling. But the message Maurice Wilkins received was that she would join his team and work under him. On her first day at King's College, Wilkins happened to be on leave. Patricia Farrar says Franklin believed she was independently in charge and was Gosling's doctoral supervisor, while Wilkins believed she worked for him, and this mismatch was the source of every problem over the following years. Their personal relationship was also extremely poor, and Farrar judges that both sides were probably equally to blame.

points.h: She was shut out of the pub and the parties
points.body: Daily life at King's College was systematic isolation for Franklin: she was not allowed into the common room for lunch, her male colleagues went to the pub after work and she could not go, and parties did not invite her. Patricia Farrar says what is written in law is not what actually happens; attitude is what matters. The only person always loyal was her PhD student Ray Gosling, and it was he who took the famous photograph; he admired her greatly. Farrar warns that these small daily exclusions can very quickly leave a person completely isolated.

points.h: The key to Photo 51 is B-form DNA
points.body: Jim Naismith explains that Wilkins had already taken DNA photographs, with samples from Switzerland of unprecedented quality, but the early images were complex and hard to interpret. Franklin's distinctive contribution was working out that the two forms of DNA — A-form (dehydrated, twisted, shorter) and B-form (hydrated, swollen) — could interconvert, and Photo 51 was of the B-form. The B-form's helical structure is very obvious, and as soon as Watson saw it and the measurements in it, he made that leap. Naismith uses the analogy of a soaked towel: wring the water out and it gets shorter and twisted, that's A-form; soak it full and it swells, that's B-form.

points.h: She was tied to A-form and missed the B-form helix
points.body: Jim Naismith offers an explanation opposite to the popular claim that "Franklin lacked imagination": she was assigned to A-form at the time, Wilkins to B-form, and Photo 51 was a B-form result that she did not give enough weight. Add to that the King's College team's refusal to cooperate, and if everyone had seen that photograph the outcome might have been different. A-form itself does not show obvious helical features, and she worried that A only became helical when it turned into B, so she was reserved about the helical structure. Crick and Watson chose to ignore that distinction. She was still the first to recognize that A-form and B-form could interconvert with humidity.

points.h: The Nobel rules mean even a living Franklin might not have won
points.body: Patricia Farrar gives two technical reasons: Franklin had already died when the Nobel was announced, and the Nobel is awarded only to the living; and the Nobel can go to at most three people. Farrar says that if she had lived, she would like to believe the prize would have gone to Watson, Crick and Franklin. But she stresses it is hard to put a number on her contribution, because at the time information came from many directions — spectroscopy, biochemistry, different methods studying the same material — it was one piece of a jigsaw.

points.h: Her virus work is the signature achievement she did alone
points.body: After leaving King's College, Franklin went to Bernal's lab at Birkbeck to study tobacco mosaic virus. Judith Howard says the atmosphere there was completely different, and drawing on the experience she had accumulated she obtained single-crystal samples and took excellent photographs. Jim Naismith adds that viruses are fascinating because they are not alive yet can transmit information, and Franklin worked out how the protein coat was organized and where the nucleic acid sat inside the virus, a key question for understanding virus structure. Howard notes that across her whole shortened career, people stare only at the less than two years of DNA.

quotes.text: What mattered isn't the number of men. It's the attitudes towards the women.

So right from the very beginning, Rosalind Franklin assumed she was working on her own in charge of Ray Gosling. She was his PhD supervisor. So Wilkins chose to assume that she was working with him and for him, and that was the source of all the problems that ensued over the next few years.
And I think it also represents two different ways of approaching science. And we tend to celebrate Watson and Crick because precisely they made this imaginative leap.

She was tied to A form. This was a B form result. She didn't give it the attention that she should have done. And that team in Kings wouldn't work as a team. Had they all looked at that, it might have been different.
But I think that what was the problem was she was never given the credit at the time as to how important that image was.
I get the impression that she would have liked to be remembered not as a woman, but as a scientist who did very, very important work in DNA, in coal, in the tobacco mosaic virus.
One thing that's missed is what a kind person she was, and she made lots of friends in science.
